speaker: Dylan Patel
title: Dylan Patel — The single biggest bottleneck to scaling AI compute
question: In AI infrastructure, why can older-generation GPUs actually retain or increase in economic value even as faster chips ship?
guest: There are two lenses to look at GPU depreciation. One lens is that if you didn't sign a long-term deal, every two years NVIDIA is tripling or quadrupling performance while only increasing price by 50% to 2x, so an H100 that was worth $2 an hour in 2024 would fall to $1 when Blackwell ramps and 70 cents when Rubin ramps. That is exactly what would happen if you could build infinite newest chips. The other lens is the utility you get out of the chip. Because you are so limited on semiconductors and deployment timelines, what prices these chips is not the comparative thing you can buy today—it's the value you can derive out of this chip today. Take GPT 5.4: it's a sparser MoE with fewer active parameters, plus advancements in training, RL, and data quality make it way better and cheaper to serve than GPT-4. So an H100 produces more tokens per GPU of a much higher-quality model with a vastly larger market, creating a dynamic where an H100 is worth more today than it was three years ago.

points.core: Leading-edge chip supply constraints prevent newer GPUs from fully replacing older fleets.
points.note: Accept: semiconductor fab bottlenecks, deployment lags, or inability to build unlimited next-generation chips keeping older GPUs in demand. Do not credit: vague statements that GPUs remain useful or generic references to high AI demand.

points.core: Scarcity prices older GPUs by their current economic output rather than replacement parity.
points.note: Accept: rental or market value being anchored to the revenue or token value a chip generates today instead of relative price-performance against newer hardware. Do not credit: generic supply-and-demand platitudes without distinguishing utility pricing from replacement-cost depreciation.

points.core: Algorithmic improvements let the same older GPU serve higher-value models more efficiently.
points.note: Accept: sparser MoE architectures, fewer active parameters, RL, or training gains increasing token throughput or intelligence value per existing GPU. Do not credit: generic claims that software gets better over time without linking it to higher output value on fixed hardware.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Older GPUs hold value because demand for compute has outrun supply, and a chip's worth depends on what it can earn, not on how it ranks against the newest model.

Several forces drive this. New chips are supply-constrained by advanced packaging, high-bandwidth memory, and above all power and data-center capacity, so an already-installed, already-powered GPU is scarce and can be rented immediately. Workloads also cascade: frontier training moves to the newest hardware, while older chips shift to inference, fine-tuning, and batch jobs, where they are perfectly adequate and demand is exploding. Software improvements keep raising the output of existing hardware too; optimized kernels, quantization, better serving stacks, and more efficient models mean an older GPU generates more tokens per hour today than when it shipped, and a mature CUDA ecosystem keeps it easy to use. Finally, once the hardware is depreciated, its ongoing cost is mostly electricity and hosting, so even lower rental rates produce strong margins.

The result has been rental prices and resale values for chips like the A100 and H100 holding up far better than expected, sometimes rising during shortages. This reverses if supply catches up or power costs dominate.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer: Older-generation GPUs retain or gain economic value because AI infrastructure is constrained more by energized data center capacity and memory than by peak compute alone. While frontier training requires the newest, tightly networked clusters, older chips cascade into booming inference, fine-tuning, and batch workloads, which are often bottlenecked by high-bandwidth memory capacity rather than raw FLOPs. Crucially, older GPUs already sit in powered, air-cooled racks, whereas newer architectures often face supply backlogs and require costly grid upgrades or liquid-cooling retrofits, making deployed silicon immediately scarce whenever demand surges. Meanwhile, software and model advances—such as optimized kernels, quantization, distillation, and sparse Mixture-of-Experts designs—steadily boost the useful throughput legacy chips deliver, effectively upgrading hardware in place. Finally, once initial capital expenditure is depreciated, operating costs fall largely to electricity and maintenance, letting operators run profitably and command higher rental or resale prices whenever aggregate AI demand outpaces new power and chip supply.

noweb.answer:
Older-generation GPUs retain or gain economic value because AI workloads cascade down the hardware stack as the market matures. While frontier model training demands the latest chips and interconnects, surging demand for inference, fine-tuning, embeddings, and smaller models prioritizes memory capacity and cost per token over peak compute. Once an older GPU’s steep upfront capital cost is depreciated, it generates revenue against little more than power and hosting expenses, letting operators undercut newer, capital-intensive clusters while earning strong margins.

Software maturation and physical bottlenecks reinforce this dynamic. Optimized kernels, quantization, and mature inference engines continually extract higher throughput from aging silicon, making the same chip more productive years after launch. Meanwhile, next-generation accelerators often require liquid cooling, high-density power retrofits, and long supply-chain lead times, whereas older GPUs already sit live in standard air-cooled racks. Whenever aggregate compute demand outpaces grid power, advanced packaging, or new data center buildouts, immediately available, amortized silicon commands a premium.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Older GPUs keep their value mainly because AI compute is still limited by supply, not by speed. Demand for tokens is growing faster than new chips, power and data-center space can be added. A GPU that is already installed, powered, cooled and networked is something a customer can use today. A new Blackwell or Rubin chip may need a building and grid connection that won't be ready for years. That's why operators like CoreWeave have reported re-signing A100 and H100 contracts at strong rates years after launch.

The work itself is also changing. Inference now makes up much of the demand, and it doesn't need the newest chips the way frontier training does. Smaller, distilled or quantized models run well on older hardware.

Software keeps improving too. Better kernels, batching, speculative decoding and serving frameworks like vLLM increase the tokens each existing GPU produces, so its earning power can rise over time.

Finally, many of these chips are partly or fully paid off. Even at lower rental prices they can be very profitable to run. As a result, they often stay in service well beyond the 3–5-year accounting lifespan skeptics assume.

Newer chips typically face long supply lead times and require high-density power and liquid cooling that existing air-cooled data centers cannot support without expensive retrofits, leaving already-deployed older fleets with a major operational advantage. At the same time, AI workloads naturally cascade down the hardware stack: even after frontier pretraining moves to newer architectures, older GPUs remain well suited for inference, fine-tuning, batch jobs, and smaller models where cost per token matters more than peak speed. Ongoing software and algorithmic advances—such as better compilers, quantization, and sparser model architectures—also increase the useful throughput of legacy chips long after they ship, effectively raising their earning power. Combined with mature software ecosystems and lower capital costs, these dynamics allow older GPUs to stay heavily utilized and command resilient, sometimes rising, rental and resale prices.

noweb.answer: Older-generation GPUs can retain or even gain economic value because AI infrastructure demand is shaped by availability, workload diversity, and total deployment cost rather than peak compute alone. When flagship chips face tight supply, long lead times, and steep prices, demand spills over to older hardware that can be deployed immediately. At the same time, the shift toward inference, fine-tuning, and smaller or quantized models creates huge workloads that do not require frontier training clusters; for these tasks, depreciated chips often deliver better performance per dollar. Continuous software improvements, such as better kernels, quantization, and serving optimizations, also increase the usable throughput of older silicon over time, boosting its revenue-generating capacity without new hardware spend. Finally, older GPUs fit smoothly into existing air-cooled data centers with standard power and networking, avoiding the expensive liquid-cooling and facility retrofits required by newer, higher-wattage chips. Combined with already-amortized capital costs, these factors keep older GPUs economically productive and can even push secondary-market and rental prices upward.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Faster GPUs raise the performance ceiling, but older GPUs can still be the cheapest way to run many AI workloads. If a model fits in an older GPU’s memory and meets its latency target, what matters is the cost per token or job, including rental, power, and cooling. A cheaper chip running near full utilization can deliver better economics than a faster chip that spends much of its time idle.

Older GPUs can also rise in value when demand for compute grows faster than new capacity comes online. If the latest chips are expensive, sold out, or waiting on data center power, customers will pay for capacity they can use today. An older fleet can then earn more through higher utilization or rental rates, which can lift resale prices even as its performance falls further behind the frontier.
